progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c05 (primary, secondary and tertiary by counting carbons on the C–OH carbon; naming alcohols; hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules; boiling points); chem-m7-c04a (hydration of ethene: steam, H₃PO₄, about 300 °C, high pressure, ⇌; HBr addition to ethene, one product; two possible products from an unsymmetrical case); chem-m7-c06 (bromoethane and aqueous hydroxide to ethanol under reflux; why reflux; distillation separates by boiling point); chem-m7-c07 (complete combustion); Module 5 (Le Chatelier: adding or removing a substance shifts an equilibrium). Year 11: balancing; oxidation as loss of electrons or hydrogen at an introductory level; electronegativity. Not assumed: dehydration, carbonyl, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid (named as products here), oxidising agent as [O].
progression.startsWith: Compare dehydration, substitution and oxidation. The video opens: Burning an alcohol completely breaks it right down, to carbon dioxide and water. Today, three reactions that turn an alcohol into a new compound instead. Here's a clue.
progression.stopsAfter: writing equations with conditions for dehydration (including two possible alkenes), substitution with HX and oxidation of alcohols; telling alcohol substitution from alkene addition; predicting aldehyde, carboxylic acid, ketone or no reaction from the class and the conditions (distil or reflux); stating the dichromate colour change and what it does and does not show. No product tests, no aldehyde and ketone naming rules or properties, no practical method.
progression.nextLesson: aldehydes and ketones, how to name them and how a test tells them apart (route chem-m7-c08, delivery part c08b).

teaching.task: Warm an orange oxidising agent with ethanol and it turns green; warm it with 2-methylpropan-2-ol and it stays orange. Where can an alcohol reaction lead, and what decides the product: the reagent, the conditions or the alcohol's class?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) burning destroys the skeleton; three other reactions keep it, and one oxidant tells two alcohols apart (1); (2) dehydration: OH plus a neighbouring H leave as water, the carbons each one bond short form C=C (2); (3) it is hydration reversed; adding water favours the alcohol, removing water favours the alkene, so the conditions are opposite, and the alkene escaping makes dehydration run one way (3); (4) different neighbours, two possible alkenes (4); (5) substitution: the halogen takes the OH's place, and the OH plus the H of HX make water; reflux keeps volatile materials in (5); (6) water as a product separates alcohol substitution from alkene addition (6); (7) oxidation removes two H atoms, giving C=O; dichromate orange to green; hazard (7); (8) the class decides: secondary has one H (ketone), tertiary none (no reaction, orange) (8); (9) primary has two: aldehyde first, and the aldehyde's carbonyl carbon still has an H, so it oxidises again to the acid; a ketone has none left, so it stops (9); (10) the aldehyde boils low (no hydrogen bonding between its molecules), so distilling removes it before further oxidation; reflux with excess oxidant returns it until it is an acid (10); (11) green shows oxidation happened, not which product or class (11); (12) the alcohol is a hub (12); memory aid (13); two attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: burning destroys an alcohol's skeleton, while one orange oxidant turns green with ethanol and stays orange with 2-methylpropan-2-ol, so the video asks where an alcohol reaction can lead and what decides the product. Dehydration takes the OH and a neighbouring hydrogen out as water so the two carbons form a C=C; it is hydration run backwards, so concentrated acid and heat replace steam and pressure, and an alcohol with two different neighbours can give two alkenes. Substitution with a hydrogen halide swaps the OH for the halogen under reflux, and the water made separates it from alkene addition of the same HBr. Oxidation removes the H of the OH and one H on its carbon to make a C=O, with acidified dichromate turning from orange to green; counting the hydrogens on the OH carbon decides the product: a secondary alcohol gives a ketone, a tertiary alcohol has none and stays orange, and a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde that still has an H and oxidises on to an acid. The aldehyde boils low because its molecules cannot hydrogen bond, so distilling catches it and reflux with excess oxidant takes it all the way; green shows oxidation, not which product. The alcohol is a hub, and the memory aid is primary goes all the way, secondary stops at ketone, tertiary won't budge. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Burning an alcohol completely breaks it right down, to carbon dioxide and water. Today, three reactions that turn an alcohol into a new compound instead. Here's a clue. This orange solution is an oxidising agent. Warm it with ethanol, and it turns green. Warm it with two-methylpropan-two-ol, another alcohol, and it stays orange. So where can an alcohol reaction lead, and what decides it?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Propan-1-ol is used in two separate experiments. In experiment 1, it is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. In experiment 2, it is heated under reflux with hydrogen bromide. For each experiment, name the organic product and identify the type of reaction." New molecule (the scenes use ethanol and butan-2-ol); tests both new reactions and their conditions. Crossed mistake: "Experiment 2: addition reaction" (the marker-reported confusion, 2025 Q24(b)). (A2) "Butan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol are each heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate solution. For each alcohol, predict the colour change and the organic product, if any. Explain the difference." New pair (scenes use propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol); tests the class rule and the reflux trap for a secondary alcohol. Crossed mistake: "Butan-2-ol under reflux → butanoic acid".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):; combustion; dehydration; substitution with HX; oxidation" Combustion was chem-m7-c07; this video covers dehydration, substitution with HX and oxidation. "investigate the products of the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols" This video predicts the products and the conditions that select them; the tests that identify the products are chem-m7-c08b, and the investigation itself is chem-m7-p04. this video starts by comparing dehydration, substitution and oxidation of an alcohol, and stops at predicting an aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid or no reaction from the alcohol's class and the conditions. It teaches: dehydration removes the OH and an H from the neighbouring carbon as water, forming a C=C bond (ethanol to ethene; conditions concentrated H₂SO₄ or concentrated H₃PO₄, about 170 °C for ethanol); dehydration is hydration (c04a) run in reverse, with opposite conditions, explained by the equilibrium (excess water favours the alcohol, removing water favours the alkene; Module 5 recall); a secondary alcohol with different neighbours can give two alkenes (butan-2-ol to but-1-ene and but-2-ene, but-2-ene usually the main product); substitution with HX swaps the OH for a halogen and the OH leaves in water (ethanol and HBr to bromoethane and water; heat under reflux, recalled from c06); telling alcohol substitution from alkene addition with the same HX (water as a product marks the alcohol reaction); oxidation removes the H of the O–H and an H from the C–OH carbon, so that carbon forms C=O (the carbonyl group, named here, taught fully in c08b); the oxidant written as [O]; acidified potassium dichromate as the oxidant, orange to green; the hazard of chromium(VI), stated once; the class decides the product because oxidation needs an H on the C–OH carbon (secondary has one: ketone; tertiary has none: no reaction, stays orange; primary has two: aldehyde, then carboxylic acid, because the aldehyde's carbonyl carbon still has an H); distil to collect the aldehyde (low boiling point, no hydrogen bonding between its molecules), reflux with excess oxidant for the acid; the green colour shows that oxidation happened, not which product; the alcohol as a hub with three exits. Not here: combustion (chem-m7-c07); naming aldehydes and ketones beyond reading the "-al" and "-one" endings, their properties and the tests that tell them apart (chem-m7-c08b); the practical procedure, apparatus details and risk table (chem-m7-p04, with `C7-IQ2-05`); mechanism names (elimination is a screen word only; "nucleophilic" is not used); Zaitsev's rule by name; cis and trans but-2-ene; the full dichromate half-equations and balanced redox equations (author note d); ether formation at lower temperature (author note b); carboxylic acid properties (chem-m7-c09); esterification (chem-m7-c10); multi-step synthesis (chem-m7-c13, g03).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c04a to c07: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; oxygen brick red, the OH ringed red as the functional group; halogens orange-brown; the new C=C or C=O second bond drawn in red as it forms; atoms about to leave ringed red; condition chips navy on and under the arrow. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Reaction 1: dehydration", "Reaction 2: substitution", "Reaction 3: oxidation", "Which product?"); centre the equation stage strip, one equation at a time, built stage by stage (reactant, reagent, arrow, conditions, products); plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 17. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous equation shrinks to a grey thumbnail or leaves before the next one builds. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 23 Oct): `m8-dichromate-orange-v1.png` and `m8-dichromate-green-v1.png` (one clear test tube in an identical single-hole wooden rack, about one third full; orange solution and green solution; the tube and rack sit in the same position in both, so they cross-fade as an aligned pair; 2000 × 2000; hook, scenes 7, 8, 11, attempt feedback 2). Before use, check the green plate's alpha: its non-transparent bounds run almost to the canvas edges (20 to 1980 px) while the orange plate's stop at 353 to 1646 px, which suggests stray semi-transparent pixels; both show a faint red-yellow matting fringe along the rack edges on a dark background (Codex asset brief). The green is a bright emerald; chromium(III) in sulfate solution is a duller blue-green, acceptable at small size (Open decisions). `m7-school-distillation-setup-v1.png` (heating mantle, round-bottom flask with a thermometer, sloping water-jacketed condenser, conical receiving flask on a third stand; 2000 × 2000; scene 10) and `m7-reflux-apparatus-v1.png` (heating mantle, round-bottom flask with an amber liquid, upright condenser with water hoses; 2000 × 2000; scenes 5 and 10), both used in c06. `m7-fume-cupboard-v1.png` not used (a chip says "fume cupboard"). Considered, not used: `m8-permanganate-purple-v1.png` and `m8-permanganate-clear-v1.png` (inspected only for size; permanganate stays a chip to keep one oxidant on screen); `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (the hook needs the reaction, not the fuel). All plates small or medium, scale uniformly only, never stretched. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The combustion thumbnail sits top-left as the hook's ethanol writes and two dichromate tube plates turn green and stay orange; the board clears to ethanol in full structural form as the water lift takes the OH and a neighbouring H out and a teal C=C draws; c04a's hydration strip returns above the dehydration strip with opposite condition chips; butan-2-ol's two neighbours glow and the strip branches into two alkenes; the swap docker lifts the OH off and docks a bromine with a grey water box; two strips set addition beside substitution with their reactants and products ringed; the hydrogen strip-off lifts two hydrogens into an [O] bubble and a red C=O draws as the dichromate plates swap colour; the H counter runs on propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol; the product ladder builds from ethanol to ethanal to ethanoic acid; boiling point chips write beside the school distillation and reflux plates; the green tube plate strikes a tertiary chip; the hub map lights its arrows in and out; the memory lines write over three small cards; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as the strips and H counter run and a crossed chip lands; the hub map and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
